summary: Describes how to do radio paging using Internet mail, focusing on pagers identified through the international telephone network, within the TPC.INT subdomain. It was replaced by RFC 1703.

eli5.summary: You email a pager number as if it were an address, and a helper turns the email into a beep.

questions: how to page someone via email
how does phone number translate to email address
subtitle: Using Internet email to send pages to radio pagers via phone numbers.

tldr.problem: Sending pages to radio pagers required special protocols and knowledge of the paging network, making it hard to integrate with email systems.
tldr.mechanism: TPC.INT uses the Internet mail infrastructure with a special domain-name format based on the pager's phone number; a mail server translates emails to page delivery instructions.
tldr.outcome: Email addresses can be used to identify and page radio pagers without requiring separate paging software or knowledge of the network details.

facts.label: Domain wildcarding
facts.value: Used for efficient routing to servers handling number prefixes

facts.label: SMTP commands
facts.value: MAIL, SEND, SOML, SAML for different latency requirements

today: RFC 1569 is obsoleted by RFC 1703. It represents an innovative approach to integrating radio paging with the Internet mail system by leveraging DNS and email. While superseded, the technique of using phone numbers as domain-based identifiers in the DNS influenced later approaches to electronic communications.

sections.title: Paging via Email
sections.content:
RFC 1569 describes a technique for delivering radio paging messages using Internet mail. Instead of using specialized paging software or protocols, the method integrates radio pagers into the standard email infrastructure by mapping pager phone numbers to email addresses.

The approach is based on the TPC.INT subdomain, a special part of the DNS namespace designed to map telephone numbers to servers. This allows pagers identified by their phone number to receive messages sent through ordinary email, making paging accessible to anyone with an email client.
sections.eli5: This memo lets you send a page to someone using email, just by using their pager's phone number in the email address. The email system automatically finds the right pager network and delivers the message.

sections.title: Pager Addresses and the TPC.INT Domain
sections.content:
A radio pager is identified by a telephone number, such as +1 415 940 8776, where "+1" is the country code. This number is transformed into an email address using the TPC.INT subdomain by reversing the digits and converting each to a domain label.

For example, the phone number +1 415 940 8776 becomes the domain 6.7.7.8.0.4.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int. The local part (the part before the @) specifies the pager type: pager-alpha for alphanumeric pagers, which can display text, or pager-numeric for numeric pagers, which display only numbers.

A complete email address might be pager-alpha@6.7.7.8.0.4.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int. The DNS uses wildcarding to route messages: a server willing to handle all phone numbers starting with +1 415 940 registers a wildcard MX record like *.0.4.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int. pointing to itself.
sections.eli5: You take the phone number, flip it backwards, put dots between the digits, and add @tpc.int. That becomes the pager's email address. The "pager-alpha" or "pager-numeric" prefix tells the server what kind of pager it is.

sections.title: How Paging Works
sections.content:
When a paging message is sent via email, the radio pager server receives the email and examines the local-part of the address. For an alphanumeric pager, the server looks at the domain-part to determine which paging network handles that phone number, then consults a local database for protocol and access details specific to that network.

For numeric pagers, the server sends only the message body, which must consist solely of digits. For alphanumeric pagers, the server decides which email headers and body content to include in the page sent to the network; some servers might send just the body, while others include the Subject line.

The RFC distinguishes between the MAIL, SEND, SOML, and SAML SMTP commands. With MAIL, a successful reply means the message is queued for transmission to the paging network. With SEND, success means the network has accepted the message for delivery. This distinction lets senders choose between guaranteed queuing and guaranteed real-time delivery.
sections.eli5: The email server looks at the phone number in the address and finds which paging network can reach that pager. It sends the message through that network. For numeric pagers, only numbers in the message are sent; for alphanumeric pagers, text is sent.

sections.title: Real-Time Paging
sections.content:
Email delivery is reliable but not guaranteed to be fast. Messages can be delayed by network problems, server queues, or mail relays, sometimes for hours. For urgent paging, this is unacceptable.

RFC 1569 addresses this by allowing clients to use the SEND or SAML SMTP commands instead of MAIL. These commands require real-time transmission on the radio network and ask the server to reply with confirmation of success or failure. Combined with direct IP connectivity from the paging client to the paging server (avoiding mail relays), this eliminates the possibility of non-deterministic delays introduced by the Internet mail infrastructure.

The trade-off is that not all servers support these commands, and direct connectivity may not always be possible. But for organizations with the capability, it provides a path to urgent, real-time paging using the familiar email infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Normal email can take a long time to arrive. If you need a page right away, you can use special SMTP commands that tell the server to deliver it to the pager immediately and confirm it worked, as long as your email server supports this.

sections.title: Paging Examples
sections.content:
An alphanumeric page might be addressed to pager-alpha@6.7.7.8.0.4.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int with a Subject line and message body. The radio pager server would read these headers and the body to construct the message sent to the paging network.

A numeric page would be addressed to pager-numeric@6.7.7.8.0.4.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int with only digits in the message body, since numeric pagers cannot display text. The server reads only the body and sends those digits to the pager.

In both cases, the message is composed as a standard RFC 822 message with a Message-ID field and appropriate content type. The paging server handles the rest, translating the email into the protocol required by the paging network.
sections.eli5: You send a normal email to the special pager address. For text pagers, include your message in the body. For numeric pagers, put numbers in the body. The paging server automatically turns that email into a page signal.
